title: Animating background-position vs transforming the layer
claim: Antipattern #22 from web-performance-antipatterns-50.md: 'animating background-position/background-size on large areas instead of transforming a layer.' This is how scrolling textures get built - parallax strips, conveyor belts, animated borders, loading stripes. The web's claim is that background-position forces a repaint where a transform is a cheap composite. animate-translate-vs-position already showed transforms skip layout entirely in cohtml; this asks whether the same holds against a background shift.
result: MARGINAL, and the verdict flips between counts, which is itself the finding. B (background-position) costs about 1.35x Script and 1.2-1.35x Styles; A (transform) is the only variant that runs UpdateNodeTransforms at all, so that phase reads A-only. Neither technique is clearly cheaper: transform moves work into the scene-graph walk, background-position moves it into style resolution and JS. Unlike animate-translate-vs-position - where transform decisively avoided a whole Layout phase - there is no clear winner here, so choose on appearance rather than cost.
notes: Applicability gate: DIRECT. background-position and background-image are both fully supported, and url() was verified manually against the Player. Rule 1: one variable, the property used to shift the artwork. Rule 2: identical DOM and geometry; both variants declare background-position in the stylesheet so neither gains a property the other lacks. Rule 3: identical JS apart from the single USE_TRANSFORM constant; both pages define both paths. Rule 4: both variants load the same pattern.png, generated by tools/make-baked-images.js at 176x128 - twice the tile size, so the background can pan a full tile width without running out of texture. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the per-frame shift IS the case and replaces the shared damage driver. Rule 7: the offset derives from the frame counter. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Paint for B against a cheap composite for A. APPEARANCE NOTE: the two are not pixel-identical - A moves the element box while B moves the artwork inside a fixed box, so the tile edges sit differently. That difference is intrinsic to the two techniques; painted area, element count and texture are the same.
